blocks.text: 1. Context Compression

blocks.alt: Selected results go through compression to become shrunk context

blocks.text: Top-K selection controls how many chunks reach the model. Context Compression covers how those selected results can be shrunk before reaching the model, attacking the token budget problem from a different angle.
It shrinks each selected chunk's text without losing the specific information a query actually needs.
2. Compressing Results, Not Just Selecting Fewer
Top-K selection, covered in Top-K Selection, controls how many chunks pass through, but too large a K dilutes context and costs tokens.
Context compression instead shrinks the content of each chunk that already passed through.

blocks.text: 3. Extracting Only The Relevant Sentences

blocks.alt: A full chunk extracts only relevant sentences

blocks.text: A long chunk often contains only one or two sentences that actually answer the query.
Extracting just those sentences keeps the useful signal while discarding the rest.
4. Summarizing Rather Than Extracting

blocks.alt: A full chunk goes through an LLM to produce a short summary

blocks.text: Instead of keeping exact sentences, a language model can generate a condensed summary of the chunk.
This trades some exact wording for an even shorter, denser representation.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Extraction preserves the chunk's exact original wording, while summarization condenses it further at the cost of losing that exact phrasing, a real tradeoff between fidelity and compactness.

blocks.text: 5. Compression Versus Too Large K Recap
Too large a K dilutes context and costs tokens, as covered in Top-K Selection. Compression attacks the same token cost problem from a different angle.
It keeps more chunks while each one individually takes up less space.
6. Risk Of Losing Important Detail

blocks.alt: Compression carries a risk of losing detail

blocks.text: An aggressive compression pass can accidentally discard a detail the model actually needed.
That risk grows as the compression ratio becomes more aggressive.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Compressing a chunk down to a single sentence risks discarding a supporting detail, like a specific date or exception, that the model needed to answer the query correctly.

blocks.text: 7. Compression Cost Versus Savings

blocks.alt: LLM call cost is compared against token savings

blocks.text: Similar to the latency cost of expansion covered in Query Expansion, running a compression model adds its own processing time.
That upfront cost has to be weighed against the tokens actually saved downstream.
8. Combining Compression With Top-K

blocks.alt: Top-K selection feeds context compression to produce the final prompt

blocks.text: As the last decision before the model, covered in Top-K Selection, compression and top-K selection work together, not as alternatives.
Selecting the right chunks, then shrinking each one, maximizes useful content per token.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Context Compression Is Worth Applying

blocks.alt: Many long chunks selected points toward using context compression

blocks.text: Long chunks with only a small relevant portion benefit most from compression.
Already short, dense chunks, by contrast, gain little from further compression.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates extracting only relevant sentences from a longer chunk.

code.content:
chunk_text = (
    "Our company was founded in 2015 in a small office space. "
    "We have grown significantly since then, expanding to three countries. "
    "Refunds are processed within five business days of the request. "
    "Our team now includes over two hundred employees worldwide."
)

query = "how long do refunds take"

def extract_relevant_sentences(query, text):
    # keep only sentences that share a word with the query
    query_words = set(query.lower().split())
    sentences = text.strip().split(". ")
    relevant = []
    for sentence in sentences:
        sentence_words = set(sentence.lower().split())
        if query_words & sentence_words:
            relevant.append(sentence.strip().rstrip("."))
    return ". ".join(relevant) + "." if relevant else ""

original_length = len(chunk_text)
compressed = extract_relevant_sentences(query, chunk_text)
compressed_length = len(compressed)

print(f"Original chunk, {original_length} characters:")
print(f"  {chunk_text!r}\n")

print(f"Compressed chunk, {compressed_length} characters:")
print(f"  {compressed!r}")

print(f"\nSize reduction: {(1 - compressed_length / original_length) * 100:.1f}%")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the chunk shrinking to just the sentence about refund timing, while discarding unrelated company history details.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Compressing so aggressively that a needed supporting detail gets discarded.
Applying compression to already short, dense chunks that gain nothing from further shrinking.
Ignoring the added latency cost of running a compression pass on every retrieved chunk.
Treating compression and top-K selection as alternatives rather than complementary techniques.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Context compression shrinks each selected chunk's text without losing needed information.
Unlike top-K selection, which controls chunk count, compression shrinks each chunk's content.
A long chunk often contains only one or two sentences that actually answer the query.
Extraction keeps exact relevant sentences; summarization condenses further with a language model.
Compression attacks the same token cost problem as top-K selection from a different angle.
Aggressive compression risks discarding a detail the model actually needed.
Running a compression model adds processing time that must be weighed against tokens saved.
Compression and top-K selection work together, maximizing useful content per token.
